Neuro-symbolic AI · Boxology · Knowledge graphs

A semantic toolbox for designing, validating, and understanding neuro-symbolic AI systems.

Say you’re building a pipeline that trains a model on labeled MRI scans and then diagnoses new ones — a neuro-symbolic (NeSy) system mixing a symbolic labeling step, a learned model, and a hybrid inference step. Today, designs like that live only in prose or a one-off diagram, so no one can check they’re actually sound, compare them to another team’s pipeline, or reuse them. Tool4Boxology fixes that: draw the pipeline with the Boxology notation, validate every step against a shared ontology, and get back a queryable knowledge graph. See it done end to end below ↓, or try it yourself: open Tool4Boxology.

Why Tool4Boxology

Neuro-symbolic architectures deserve a shared, checkable language.

General-purpose modelling tools such as UML diagrams or ML-pipeline editors don't capture what a neuro-symbolic component actually is, and they don't enforce whether an architecture is structurally or semantically valid. Boxology closes that gap.

Boxology, made precise

Boxology is a typed visual notation — introduced by van Harmelen et al. in "Modular Design Patterns for Hybrid Learning and Reasoning Systems" (2023) — for describing hybrid AI systems as elementary patterns of data, symbols, actors, processes, and models. Tool4Boxology turns that notation into something you can draw, validate, and check automatically, not just read.

From sketch to knowledge graph

Every design moves through three connected layers: a design layer where the editor enforces syntax as you draw, a knowledge representation layer where an RML pipeline and the T4B ontology turn the validated diagram into an RDF knowledge graph, and an exploration layer where SPARQL and SHACL let you query and check that graph.

Getting started

Open the local editor, then go from a blank canvas to a queryable knowledge graph in six steps.

The editor runs locally during development. Once it's running, everything below happens in one browser tab: shapes on the left, canvas in the middle, properties on the right. (See the Tumor Diagnosis example below for what the finished result looks like.)

Launch the editor

Start the interface, then open it locally.

Run npm run dev from Boxology-Interface (or docker-compose up for the full pipeline with Virtuoso), then open the running app in your browser.

Open editor — localhost:5173
Running on a different port or host? Swap in whatever address your terminal prints when Vite starts.

Select components

Open the Shapes panel on the left and pick from Data & Information, Actors & Entities, AI & Models, or Processes & Actions — or start faster from the Elementary Patterns library — then drop your pick onto the canvas.

Connect & cluster

Connect components to form Input → Process → Output triples, then select a complete triple and right-click to group it into a cluster.

Annotate semantics

Select a node in the Properties panel on the right and set its semantic type — Data, Symbol, Actor, Model, or a process such as Train, Deduce, Transform, or Engineer.

Validate

Click Validate in the toolbar to check the selected pattern (or the whole diagram) against Tool4Boxology's structural and semantic rules.

Generate the KG

Click Create KG to send the diagram through the RML pipeline and populate the Virtuoso-backed knowledge graph.

Explore with SPARQL

Open the SPARQL editor or the KG Viewer from the toolbar to query, inspect, and reuse the knowledge graph you just created.

Inside the editor

The workspace is split into three panes, each collapsible with Ctrl+Alt+[ (left) and Ctrl+Alt+] (right):

  • Shapes & patterns — categorized components plus reusable elementary and custom patterns.
  • Canvas — drag, connect, and cluster nodes across multiple diagram pages (tabs at the top).
  • Properties — rename elements and assign their semantic type once selected.

Toolbar & file formats

Save and reopen work as .boxology files, undo/redo freely, and export to PNG, JPG, JSON, or DOT (opens directly in Graphviz). The same toolbar creates the knowledge graph and opens the KG Viewer once it exists.

Feature overview

The four pieces that turn a diagram into a checkable, queryable knowledge graph.

Every screen in the editor traces back to a specific part of the underlying pipeline described in the paper.

01

Visual editor

Compose architectures by dragging elementary patterns — data, symbol, actor, process, model — onto the canvas and wiring them into Input → Process → Output triples.

02

Semantic validation

Diagrams are checked against structural rules and the T4B ontology, so mismatches and incomplete structures are caught while the model is still easy to adjust.

03

Knowledge graph export

An RDF Mapping Language (RML) pipeline turns a validated diagram into an RDF knowledge graph, making the architecture machine-readable.

04

Interactive KG Viewer

Explore the graph visually, and click any pattern to see a live valid/invalid check with its inputs and outputs — see it below.

See it in practice

One real pipeline, from sketch to a validated answer.

Here's the whole loop on a real design we call Tumor Diagnosis: an MRI-based diagnosis pipeline drawn, validated, and queried in Tool4Boxology.

The design

Three composed patterns, one pipeline

An Expert engineers labels for MRI segments (Labeling); those labels, combined with preprocessed scan data, train a model (Train a Supervised Model); the trained model then deduces a diagnosis from a new scan (Symptom Detection). Each stage is named by its epistemic role — engineering, training, deducing — not drawn as a generic, unlabeled box.

Validate

Check Boxology confirms all three patterns match legal typed combinations in the T4B ontology: Engineer: [Actor]→[Symbol], Train: [Symbol,Data]→[Model], Deduce: [Data,Model]→[Symbol]. Not just a plausible-looking flowchart — a well-formed neuro-symbolic system.

Query

Once it's a knowledge graph, ask it questions directly. "Which pattern produced Label for Segments?" becomes one SPARQL query — no re-reading the diagram, no guessing.

Get an answer

The graph returns exactly one row: the Labeling pattern. That's the practical payoff — a design you can interrogate, not just look at.

Every pattern checked against the ontology — all three come back valid.
The SPARQL answer: Labeling produced Label for Segments.
Exploration layer

Every pattern in the knowledge graph documents and validates itself.

Open a generated knowledge graph in the built-in KG Viewer to explore it as a live network, not just a query result — drag nodes, zoom, search, and click any pattern to see whether it's valid and why.

Click a pattern, get its documentation

Selecting a design-pattern node opens a detail panel with its Type, a live VALID / INVALID status, the formal validation pattern it matched, and its exact inputs and outputs — the same rules the editor's validator checks, applied directly to the graph. Below, the Tumor Diagnosis graph from the example above, with Train a Supervised Model selected: VALID, matching Symbol-Data>Train>Model, inputs Label for Segments and Preprocessed MRT Data, output Supervised Model. Edit the diagram later and accidentally break a pattern, and this is where you'd see it flip to invalid.

Need documentation for the whole system instead of one pattern? Generate Documentation turns the current knowledge graph into a written summary you can share or archive.

Filter by type or label, search for a node by name, and export the current view as Visual JSON or a PNG snapshot.

Research

Published at ESWC 2026 — read the paper behind the tool.

Tool4Boxology is the reference implementation for a peer-reviewed method for making neuro-symbolic architectures semantic, valid, and interoperable.

Tool4Boxology: A Semantic Toolbox for Constructing and Analysing Neuro-Symbolic Architectures

Johannes E. Bendler1, Yashrajsinh Chudasama2,3, Mahsa Forghani2,3, Enrique Iglesias2,4, Disha Purohit2,3, Jacquiline Roney1, Annette ten Teije1, Frank van Harmelen1, Maria-Esther Vidal2,3 — ESWC 2026, Springer-Verlag, pp. 191–211.

1 Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam · 2 TIB – Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology · 3 Leibniz University Hannover · 4 L3S Research Center, Hannover

"Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) AI systems are increasingly used in domains such as healthcare and finance, yet their architectures are often described only in prose or diagrams, making them difficult to compare, reproduce, or integrate. Existing modelling tools, such as UML or ML workflow editors, do not capture the semantics of NeSy components or enforce syntactic and semantic constraints on architectural validity." The paper validates the approach on 61 neuro-symbolic systems from biomedical literature plus 7 from other domains.
